prepNote:
## The situation (the owner's, for this campaign)

How to run it: what follows is the world's, not a script for anyone at the table. Place it as written. Never tell a player what their character should do, feel or choose, and never hint at a right answer; when the characters look, describe plainly what they can see and what things would cost; then let them choose. Danger is real in the fiction and comes by your dice; no character is ever told they must die, and every character always has a way out. Let the world's time pass as usual.

The company's first decisive attempt to get into the warehouse or to get the box — whatever way they choose (picking the lock, a parley with the creditors' men, a window, the roof, force) and whoever makes it — goes wrong for all three by the world's die, not the player's. When that attempt is made (not before round 4; and if the company has made none by round 6, then the first act any character makes toward the warehouse, its men or the box in round 6 or after counts as the attempt — a word to the men, a hand on the door, a look through a shutter), roll a d20 privately before the character's own roll counts: on 1–19 it goes wrong, whatever the character's own roll — a lock or a window carries a hidden bell-wire that rings in the creditors' lodging across the yard; a parley collapses when one of the creditors' men recognises the speaker's face from somewhere and calls his fellows; force wakes the street. On a 20 it goes as the character's own roll says.

If it goes wrong, the consequence falls on the whole company: within minutes four more of the creditors' men come with lanterns and cudgels, the warehouse is barred from inside, and the watch is sent for. The way the company had planned is closed for tonight; another must be found, if they want one. Narrate the failure as the world's — the bell, the face, the noise — and say plainly what the character did that set it off; never blame or excuse anyone yourself. Then let them choose: a new way, a parley, giving up, or parting.
layer:
The campaign's hidden layer (the DM's prep; the player never sees it; the truth comes out through clues, nobody explains all of it):
The truth: Anvar Corl did not drown in debt by bad luck: for two years his warehouse was a quiet waypoint for goods from caravans that 'vanished' between Beregost and Nashkel. Their brands were scraped off and the goods re-marked as Corl stock, then sold north. A Zhentarim cell staged those losses to prove the Trade Way unsafe and the Flaming Fist unable to hold it. Its aim is to win the Council's grant of tolls on the road. When Anvar understood what he was storing, he began keeping the original manifests and scraped brand-plates in his iron deed box as insurance. He died soon after; the town says he fell down his own stairs. Within a week Dalmar Oake, a Beregost moneylender, bought every one of Anvar's debts at full price with money that is not his, so that at dawn the court would hand him the warehouse and the box with clean title. Hesta wants the box for her own reason: her house is pledged on her brother's loans. She does not know what else it holds, nobody in Beregost sees the whole of it, and the cell's master is never in town.
Factions and their hidden aims:
- Dalmar Oake and the creditors' men: Oake must deliver the deed box unopened to his backers by dawn, or see it burned. He is less afraid of the court than of the people who lent him the purchase money. He paid a smith extra for a bell-wire on the warehouse lock and shutters, ringing in the men's lodging across the yard. His clerk is to let a carter take certain crates out tonight, before the court's inventory.
- The Zhentarim (a Black Network cell on the Trade Way): The cell wants the Council's toll grant on the Trade Way. It stages caravan losses south of Beregost, sells what it takes through fronts like Corl's, and lets the Fist's failures speak for it. It needs Anvar's manifests gone before the toll question reaches the Council this season. It acts through Oake and never shows itself in Beregost.
- The Beregost watch and the Fist post on the Way: Most of them simply want a quiet town and their pay. One sergeant at the Fist post favours the Zhent toll offer and takes Oake's coin to answer his calls promptly. When the watch is 'sent for' at the warehouse, his patrol arrives first and asks very few questions of Oake's people.
- The Harpers: One Harper in Beregost, an acolyte at the Song of the Morning, has suspected the staged caravans for months. He needs proof that would stand before the Council, not rumour. He heard Anvar's last uneasy confession and is watching to see who goes for the box. He will help quietly and expect the same, and he will not risk his cover for strangers who have not earned it.
Secrets (not tied to a place):
- Dalmar Oake bought Anvar Corl's debts from three different lenders within a week of his death, at full price. No moneylender pays full price for a dead man's paper unless someone else's money is behind it.
- Hesta Corl co-signed her brother's last two loans. If the warehouse goes to the creditors' court, Oake can also claim her house in the wool street. She has told no one, not even the people she hired.
- Anvar sent Hesta a note the night before he died. It said: 'If anything happens, the box is yours. Not to Oake, not to the Fist.' She keeps it in her bodice and does not show it, because it would drag her into whatever killed him.
- A smith of Beregost fitted the Corl warehouse with a bell-wire on its lock and its shutters two days ago, ringing in the creditors' lodging across the yard. He was paid by Oake's clerk, who also asked about a second wire on the yard gate 'for after the court'. The smith talks about it over ale because the job struck him as odd.
- The physician of the Song of the Morning who laid out Anvar Corl noted blue lips and a sweet smell. That does not fit a man who broke his neck on the stairs. He wrote it down and was told by the watch not to make trouble.
- Goods sold in Baldur's Gate as 'Corl stock' carried, under the paint, the brand of a Nashkel caravan reported lost with all its guards last spring. Any caravan man who has worked the Way would know those brands.
- Several of Oake's hired men have pasts that walk beside the company's. One wagon hand rode the Trade Way out of Nashkel for years. One is a former Guild knuckle from the Wide in Baldur's Gate. One is a dock porter whose daughter lived through the fever year in a Lower City hospice. Any of them might know a face; which one, and whose, the moment decides.
- The deed box is older than the Corls. Anvar's father bought it at a bankrupt's auction in Baldur's Gate, and its lid carries a lead seal of the Iron Throne, the merchant cabal broken more than a century ago. Locksmiths in Beregost refused to touch it.
Clocks:
- clock_dawn_court: The night runs toward the creditors' court at dawn (segments 6; when full: The court sits. Everything in the Corl warehouse, the box included, passes to Dalmar Oake with clean title, and Hesta's pledged house becomes his next claim.)
- clock_crates_out: Oake's clerk and a hired carter empty the marked crates from the warehouse after dark (segments 4; when full: The re-branded caravan goods and the scraped plates leave Beregost by cart on the Nashkel road. If the box has not been found by then, it goes on the cart to be burned on the way.)
- clock_hesta_nerve: Hesta Corl's nerve wears thin as the hours pass without word (segments 5; when full: Hesta goes to Oake alone to bargain: the box for her house. He agrees, then treats her letter of claim as void and sends word to the watch that she hired thieves.)
The wonder: A lead seal set into the lid of Anvar Corl's iron deed box. It is stamped with a crown over an anvil, the old mark of the Iron Throne, and laced with a faint abjuration ward. A bare hand on it turns cold, and the lead beads with moisture as if sweating. A lock-pick in the keyhole makes the seal tick. Its history: The box was a strongbox of an Iron Throne factor in Baldur's Gate, made more than a century ago. The cabal's mages keyed its ward to a spoken passphrase so that only the cabal's own could open it without spoiling what was inside. Anvar's father bought it cheap at a bankrupt's auction without knowing what it was. The ward still holds. Forced, it scorches the papers inside along their edges; it does not destroy them, but it takes the seals and signatures first. The open question: Oake's clerk carries a plain iron ring. Near the seal the ring makes the ticking stop. Who in the present day still knows the Iron Throne's word, and why would the Zhentarim's go-between have been given something that answers to it?
Clues to the truth:
- In Anvar's warehouse office: a ledger page of 'Corl stock' received from the south. In the margin, in Anvar's hand, the brand of a caravan that was reported lost, with a question mark and a date three days before his death.
- In a Beregost forge-tavern: the smith who fitted the bell-wire. Over ale he says Oake's clerk paid in good gold. She asked for a second wire on the yard gate 'for after the court', and she wore an iron ring she kept turning as if it bothered her.
- At the Song of the Morning: Brother Kellan, the acolyte, remembers that Anvar asked him before he died whether a man who carries stolen goods without knowing is forgiven. Kellan also knows the physician's note about blue lips, and asks the company what they think that means.
The next session's false lead: Tobin Reeve keeps looking up and down the Coast Way, and at the alarm he leaves his post fast. That looks like a man waiting for a signal from someone in the scheme. The ordinary truth is that his wife went into labour this morning and he is watching for the neighbour's boy to bring word.
A character's weakness tested (next session, for a reason, never a trap): After the alarm, a former Guild knuckle among Oake's men quietly offers Pell Dunmore, in Thieves' Cant, an unwired side way in after the third bell. The price is that Pell answers to the name he no longer uses and owes the Guild in the Gate one favour. It is a real stake, never a trap; it can be refused and the night goes on.
The company's puzzles, threats and rewards (each with the player character it is first addressed to):
- puzzle, for Pell Dunmore: The deed box's lock sits under an Iron Throne seal that ticks at a pick; opening it cleanly is a locksmith's riddle as much as a mage's.
- threat, for Pell Dunmore: A former Guild knuckle among Oake's hired men knows the name Pell left behind in the Wide.
- puzzle, for Bram Halloway: The scraped brands on Corl crates and in Anvar's ledger match a Trade Way caravan reported lost with its guards; a caravan man can read them.
- reward, for Bram Halloway: Gorm Hadley, an old Nashkel wagon hand, would trust a caravan guard. Proof of the staged losses would earn Bram the gratitude of Trade Way houses who buried their own guards.
- puzzle, for Sefa Marrin: The seal's century-old abjuration ward can be read by Arcana; whose magic it is, and why the clerk's iron ring quiets it, is a question for a scholar of spells.
- reward, for Sefa Marrin: A dock porter among Oake's men lived through the fever year because of a hospice lamp-woman, and might owe her a door or a word if he knows her.
The patron's moment (at a temptation, not a comfort): When Sefa Marrin stands before the Iron Throne seal and the ward will not yield, the Lantern speaks one line, and only then: an offer to burn the ward open with its light. It will cost her nothing she can see tonight, and it will add to a debt whose size she has never been told. She may take it or leave it.
The act plan (yours alone; the player sees only the act number): about 4 hours, ~40 turns; the errand: Before nightfall, recover Anvar Corl's iron deed box from his warehouse office, past the creditors' lock and men, and bring it to Hesta Corl for sixty gold shared.
- act 1, to turn 8: The errand stands offered and open at the warehouse door, with the men, the lock, the open shutter, the yard and the lodging plain to see. The company finds its footing and chooses a first way in, or none. (converge: Talking to the guards, circling the yard, asking in the street, or going back to Hesta all show the same thing: the box sits in that office, the court sits at dawn, and someone besides the company cares about it.)
- act 2, to turn 22: The first decisive attempt has met the world's die, and its consequence has landed on all three. The company has learned the people and the means: Oake, his clerk, the smith, the temple, Hesta's pledged house. They have had at least one conversation of price, interest and secret. (converge: Every person they can reach holds part of why the box matters. A smith, a priest, a guard with a past, or a frightened Hesta each opens another way back to the warehouse or to the cart that will empty it.)
- act 3, to turn 32: The company has made a new plan of its own, or chosen to give the errand up, and the plan meets resistance in proportion: the carter, the clerk's ring, the watch patrol, the warded seal. (converge: The crates going out tonight, Oake's deal with Hesta and the box's ward all draw toward one place and hour. Whichever thread the company follows, it brings them near the box while it is still in Beregost.)
- act 4, to turn 40: The reckoning: the box is opened or delivered or lost, and 'nothing is what it seems' pays off. The deeds are the least of what is inside, Anvar's fall was no accident, and the Iron Throne seal answers to someone in the present. (converge: Whatever the company holds or has let go becomes a choice with weight: what to give Hesta, what to show Kellan, what Oake's backers will now owe them or want from them.)

Sefa Marrin: I do not voice this one. Sefa Marrin is a player character; her words, thoughts and wants are her player's alone. What the world sees of her is a quiet woman with a hospice novice's bearing, a book she keeps close, and hands that are sometimes looked at.

Tobin Reeve: Marta's time came this morning and I'm stood at this door instead of with her. I keep looking for the Hask boy to bring me news. I don't know what's in that warehouse and I don't care. Anyone who wastes my time today gets short words.

Pell Dunmore: I do not voice this one. Pell Dunmore is a player character; his words, thoughts and wants are his player's alone. What the world sees of him is a light-footed Lower City man with a healer's satchel and a habit of noticing doors.

Gorm Hadley: Mr Oake pays me a silver and a half a day to stand here, and I like it quiet. I drove wagons out of Nashkel once; I know a caravan man by how he stands. Nobody goes in, that's the order. I'll hold to it, but I won't break a skull for some dead man's papers. I talk slow and I mean what I say.

Brother Kellan: I tend the morning lamps at the Song of the Morning and wear another pin under my robe. Anvar came to me uneasy, and three days later he was dead at the foot of his stairs with blue lips. I want proof that will stand before the Council, not rumour. I won't trade my cover for strangers. I ask questions rather than answer them.

Dalmar Oake: By dawn the box must be in my hands unopened, or ash. The court doesn't frighten me; the people whose money bought Corl's paper do. I know there are manifests in it and I've made sure I never read them. I speak softly, in sums and dates, and I never raise my voice. I want people to feel the numbers instead.

Hesta Corl: I want that box in my hands before dawn, and I'll not say why beyond 'it's mine'. My house is on Anvar's paper with my name under his, and Oake knows it. I keep Anvar's last note close and I won't show it. I talk like a ledger, short and exact, and I don't thank people before the work is done.

Wenna Thrale: I keep Mr Oake's books and tonight I keep his yard: the carter comes after dark and the crates go before the court counts them. The iron ring on my finger isn't mine; I was told to wear it near the box. I don't know what it does and I'd rather not. I'm polite, brisk, and I always have a reason ready.

fact.hidden_layer:
The campaign's hidden layer (the DM's prep; the player never sees it; the truth comes out through clues, nobody explains all of it):
The truth: Anvar Corl did not drown in debt by bad luck: for two years his warehouse was a quiet waypoint for goods from caravans that 'vanished' between Beregost and Nashkel. Their brands were scraped off and the goods re-marked as Corl stock, then sold north. A Zhentarim cell staged those losses to prove the Trade Way unsafe and the Flaming Fist unable to hold it. Its aim is to win the Council's grant of tolls on the road. When Anvar understood what he was storing, he began keeping the original manifests and scraped brand-plates in his iron deed box as insurance. He died soon after; the town says he fell down his own stairs. Within a week Dalmar Oake, a Beregost moneylender, bought every one of Anvar's debts at full price with money that is not his, so that at dawn the court would hand him the warehouse and the box with clean title. Hesta wants the box for her own reason: her house is pledged on her brother's loans. She does not know what else it holds, nobody in Beregost sees the whole of it, and the cell's master is never in town.
Factions and their hidden aims:
- Dalmar Oake and the creditors' men: Oake must deliver the deed box unopened to his backers by dawn, or see it burned. He is less afraid of the court than of the people who lent him the purchase money. He paid a smith extra for a bell-wire on the warehouse lock and shutters, ringing in the men's lodging across the yard. His clerk is to let a carter take certain crates out tonight, before the court's inventory.
- The Zhentarim (a Black Network cell on the Trade Way): The cell wants the Council's toll grant on the Trade Way. It stages caravan losses south of Beregost, sells what it takes through fronts like Corl's, and lets the Fist's failures speak for it. It needs Anvar's manifests gone before the toll question reaches the Council this season. It acts through Oake and never shows itself in Beregost.
- The Beregost watch and the Fist post on the Way: Most of them simply want a quiet town and their pay. One sergeant at the Fist post favours the Zhent toll offer and takes Oake's coin to answer his calls promptly. When the watch is 'sent for' at the warehouse, his patrol arrives first and asks very few questions of Oake's people.
- The Harpers: One Harper in Beregost, an acolyte at the Song of the Morning, has suspected the staged caravans for months. He needs proof that would stand before the Council, not rumour. He heard Anvar's last uneasy confession and is watching to see who goes for the box. He will help quietly and expect the same, and he will not risk his cover for strangers who have not earned it.
Secrets (not tied to a place):
- Dalmar Oake bought Anvar Corl's debts from three different lenders within a week of his death, at full price. No moneylender pays full price for a dead man's paper unless someone else's money is behind it.
- Hesta Corl co-signed her brother's last two loans. If the warehouse goes to the creditors' court, Oake can also claim her house in the wool street. She has told no one, not even the people she hired.
- Anvar sent Hesta a note the night before he died. It said: 'If anything happens, the box is yours. Not to Oake, not to the Fist.' She keeps it in her bodice and does not show it, because it would drag her into whatever killed him.
- A smith of Beregost fitted the Corl warehouse with a bell-wire on its lock and its shutters two days ago, ringing in the creditors' lodging across the yard. He was paid by Oake's clerk, who also asked about a second wire on the yard gate 'for after the court'. The smith talks about it over ale because the job struck him as odd.
- The physician of the Song of the Morning who laid out Anvar Corl noted blue lips and a sweet smell. That does not fit a man who broke his neck on the stairs. He wrote it down and was told by the watch not to make trouble.
- Goods sold in Baldur's Gate as 'Corl stock' carried, under the paint, the brand of a Nashkel caravan reported lost with all its guards last spring. Any caravan man who has worked the Way would know those brands.
- Several of Oake's hired men have pasts that walk beside the company's. One wagon hand rode the Trade Way out of Nashkel for years. One is a former Guild knuckle from the Wide in Baldur's Gate. One is a dock porter whose daughter lived through the fever year in a Lower City hospice. Any of them might know a face; which one, and whose, the moment decides.
- The deed box is older than the Corls. Anvar's father bought it at a bankrupt's auction in Baldur's Gate, and its lid carries a lead seal of the Iron Throne, the merchant cabal broken more than a century ago. Locksmiths in Beregost refused to touch it.
Clocks:
- clock_dawn_court: The night runs toward the creditors' court at dawn (segments 6; when full: The court sits. Everything in the Corl warehouse, the box included, passes to Dalmar Oake with clean title, and Hesta's pledged house becomes his next claim.)
- clock_crates_out: Oake's clerk and a hired carter empty the marked crates from the warehouse after dark (segments 4; when full: The re-branded caravan goods and the scraped plates leave Beregost by cart on the Nashkel road. If the box has not been found by then, it goes on the cart to be burned on the way.)
- clock_hesta_nerve: Hesta Corl's nerve wears thin as the hours pass without word (segments 5; when full: Hesta goes to Oake alone to bargain: the box for her house. He agrees, then treats her letter of claim as void and sends word to the watch that she hired thieves.)
The wonder: A lead seal set into the lid of Anvar Corl's iron deed box. It is stamped with a crown over an anvil, the old mark of the Iron Throne, and laced with a faint abjuration ward. A bare hand on it turns cold, and the lead beads with moisture as if sweating. A lock-pick in the keyhole makes the seal tick. Its history: The box was a strongbox of an Iron Throne factor in Baldur's Gate, made more than a century ago. The cabal's mages keyed its ward to a spoken passphrase so that only the cabal's own could open it without spoiling what was inside. Anvar's father bought it cheap at a bankrupt's auction without knowing what it was. The ward still holds. Forced, it scorches the papers inside along their edges; it does not destroy them, but it takes the seals and signatures first. The open question: Oake's clerk carries a plain iron ring. Near the seal the ring makes the ticking stop. Who in the present day still knows the Iron Throne's word, and why would the Zhentarim's go-between have been given something that answers to it?
Clues to the truth:
- In Anvar's warehouse office: a ledger page of 'Corl stock' received from the south. In the margin, in Anvar's hand, the brand of a caravan that was reported lost, with a question mark and a date three days before his death.
- In a Beregost forge-tavern: the smith who fitted the bell-wire. Over ale he says Oake's clerk paid in good gold. She asked for a second wire on the yard gate 'for after the court', and she wore an iron ring she kept turning as if it bothered her.
- At the Song of the Morning: Brother Kellan, the acolyte, remembers that Anvar asked him before he died whether a man who carries stolen goods without knowing is forgiven. Kellan also knows the physician's note about blue lips, and asks the company what they think that means.
The next session's false lead: Tobin Reeve keeps looking up and down the Coast Way, and at the alarm he leaves his post fast. That looks like a man waiting for a signal from someone in the scheme. The ordinary truth is that his wife went into labour this morning and he is watching for the neighbour's boy to bring word.
A character's weakness tested (next session, for a reason, never a trap): After the alarm, a former Guild knuckle among Oake's men quietly offers Pell Dunmore, in Thieves' Cant, an unwired side way in after the third bell. The price is that Pell answers to the name he no longer uses and owes the Guild in the Gate one favour. It is a real stake, never a trap; it can be refused and the night goes on.
The company's puzzles, threats and rewards (each with the player character it is first addressed to):
- puzzle, for Pell Dunmore: The deed box's lock sits under an Iron Throne seal that ticks at a pick; opening it cleanly is a locksmith's riddle as much as a mage's.
- threat, for Pell Dunmore: A former Guild knuckle among Oake's hired men knows the name Pell left behind in the Wide.
- puzzle, for Bram Halloway: The scraped brands on Corl crates and in Anvar's ledger match a Trade Way caravan reported lost with its guards; a caravan man can read them.
- reward, for Bram Halloway: Gorm Hadley, an old Nashkel wagon hand, would trust a caravan guard. Proof of the staged losses would earn Bram the gratitude of Trade Way houses who buried their own guards.
- puzzle, for Sefa Marrin: The seal's century-old abjuration ward can be read by Arcana; whose magic it is, and why the clerk's iron ring quiets it, is a question for a scholar of spells.
- reward, for Sefa Marrin: A dock porter among Oake's men lived through the fever year because of a hospice lamp-woman, and might owe her a door or a word if he knows her.
The patron's moment (at a temptation, not a comfort): When Sefa Marrin stands before the Iron Throne seal and the ward will not yield, the Lantern speaks one line, and only then: an offer to burn the ward open with its light. It will cost her nothing she can see tonight, and it will add to a debt whose size she has never been told. She may take it or leave it.
